newsitem.title: UK: Britain dismisses reports of U.S. snub on Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Britain dismisses reports of U.S. snub on Ireland.

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Patrick Mayhew on Thursday dismissed media reports that he was being snubbed by U.S. secretary of State Madeleine Albright in a row over policy in Northern Ireland.

Newspapers in Britain and Ireland said Albright had cancelled a meeting with Mayhew during her visit to London next week due to anger at what has been interpreted in Washington as British attempts to manipulate U.S. policy.
Mayhew told BBC radio on Thursday he had been scheduled to meet Albright and the meeting had in fact been cancelled.
But he said: "I don't think it's a snub at all.
"Madeleine Albright asked to see me, I didn't ask to see Madeleine Albright. Then the ambassador told me there are difficulties (about her timetable)...
"I look forward to seeing Madeleine Albright. She will be seeing the prime minister."

A U.S. embassy spokesman said Albright had orginally been intended to meet Mayhew, but this had become impossible due to scheduling difficulties. He rejected any suggestion that Albright was snubbing Mayhew by not seeing him.

The London Times and the Irish Times quoted U.S. diplomatic sources as saying the decision to cancel the meeting was a retaliation for British media reports that Albright was going to withdraw Jean Kennedy Smith as U.S. ambassador to Ireland.

These reports also said Albright would decisively throw her weight behind Britain's refusal to let the Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein, into peace talks without a renewed IRA ceasefire, distancing Washington from Sinn Fein.
But the Irish Times said Albright saw this as a British engineered story to manipulate U.S. policy.
A White House spokesman said on Monday that the United States had no plans to recall Kennedy Smith or to make major changes in its Ireland policy.

"There are certainly no plans to recall Ambassador Smith and the United States maintains its intense interest, which starts at the president, in doing whatever we can in helping the people of Ireland to find peace," said spokesman David Johnson.
"The suggestions that we are considering sharp changes in our policy are absolutely false," he said.
Mayhew said Washington and London were agreed on policy, but he added: "The line from Washington has been a very different one since the ending of the (IRA) ceasefire in February."
Northern Ireland was pushed closer to the brink of sectarian war on Wednesday when a suspected IRA sniper killed a British soldier at the southern village of Bessbrook.

British Prime Minister John Major pledged to track down the guilty and punish the "murderous efforts" of the IRA which he blamed for the killing of the 23-year-old. Gerry Adams, President of Sinn Fein, said the shooting was "a tragic event which re-emphasises the need for for all of us to redouble our efforts to rebuild the peace process."
But British and Irish officials accused him of hypocrisy by expressing regret for an action they blame on his IRA supporters, who share Sinn Fein's goal of ending British rule.
